Beyond Discrimination: A Matched-Control
Pathway Audit for Evaluating Pathway-Specific
Evidence in ECG Classifiers
Anonymous
Abstract—Objective: We test whether ECG classifiers rely
on clinically meaningful signal regions—rather than statistically
correlated but mechanistically irrelevant shortcuts—by auditing
their pathway dependence against medical knowledge, and we
assess whether such pathway-specific evidence survives cross￾dataset transfer.
Methods: We propose a model-agnostic matched-control per￾turbation audit grounded in clinical ECG diagnostic crite￾ria. For five diagnoses spanning timing (1AVB), morphol￾ogy (CRBBB/CLBBB), and rhythm (SBRAD/AFIB) pathways,
we predefine disease-relevant target regions and anatomically
matched control regions following standard ECG interpreta￾tion rules. The Anatomical Specificity Score (ASS) requires
the effect of target-region perturbation to exceed that of the
strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than perturbation
sensitivity alone. The protocol uses linear interpolation as the
primary perturbation operator (selected via a preregistered four￾operator comparison battery), and validates pathway conclusions
under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% (345,779 exams)
to an independent cardiologist-validated dataset (PTB-XL fold
10). Each (architecture, disease) pair is assigned to one of
three evidence tiers: Pathway-supported, Evidence-limited, or
Not supported. Four architectures (XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet,
Transformer) at three representation levels are evaluated.
Results: Discrimination was high across all three raw-signal
architectures—ResNet, for instance, achieved AUROC> 0.98 for
all five diseases, and frozen-weight transfer preserved AUROC>
0.93 for all diseases across all three architectures. Yet under
the primary matched-control perturbation operator, only 6 of
these 15 model-disease pairs reached Pathway-supported, with 1
Evidence-limited and 8 Not supported. QRS-morphology path￾ways (CRBBB, CLBBB) were the consistent positive finding: all
three architectures reached Pathway-supported on both datasets,
with positive internal and external ASS across all 6 pairs (external
ASS range: CRBBB 0.255–0.455; CLBBB 0.261–0.387; CI> 0 on
both datasets). For 1AVB, all three architectures yielded negative
ASS under the primary operator on both datasets—the matched
QRS control consistently exceeded the PR-segment target effect
(e.g., ResNet internal ASS= −0.332; external ASS= −0.278),
a false-positive pathway claim that target-only perturbation
would have produced. AFIB atrial-window ASS was negative
across all three architectures and both datasets. SBRAD rate￾pathway evidence was architecture-dependent: ResNet reached
Evidence-limited (positive ASS on both datasets but external
CI crosses zero), while SE-ResNet and Transformer were Not
supported. XGBoost, operating on handcrafted features, provided
complementary feature-space evidence outside the waveform
perturbation tiering. The operator-comparison battery revealed
that zero-masking inflated control-region disruption and could
reverse pathway conclusions. Conclusion: We present a medical￾knowledge-informed auditing methodology capable of system￾atically evaluating ECG pathway dependence in classification
models and assessing their cross-dataset transferability, demon￾strated across four architectures spanning three representation
levels. With explicit operator selection and external validation, the
matched-control protocol separates disease-consistent signal use
from two confounds: statistically correlated but mechanistically
irrelevant shortcuts, and operator-induced artifacts. It thereby
provides an evaluation axis that is clinically interpretable and
complements conventional discrimination metrics. Pathway con￾clusions depend on the predefined anatomical regions, the per￾turbation operator, and the datasets used; the current evidence is
limited to five diagnoses across two datasets. The matched-control
audit principle may extend to other biomedical signal domains
where clinically meaningful input regions can be defined a priori.
Index Terms—ECG classification, explanation evaluation,
matched-control perturbation, pathway audit, operator compar￾ison, cross-dataset transfer, pathway-specific evidence, patient￾level validation
I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we pre￾specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR segment
for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block) and
compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adjacent
control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim is
accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to
cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, providing an external
check on whether explanation conclusions are dataset-specific.
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and

We instantiate the audit across four model architectures
(XGBoost, ResNet, SE-ResNet, and a lightweight Trans￾former) at three representation levels—simple summary fea￾tures, timing-enriched handcrafted features, and raw signal—
to assess whether pathway dependence is consistent across

Our primary contribution is the audit protocol itself—a
structured method for evaluating whether ECG classifiers base
decisions on disease-relevant signal regions, rather than on
correlated but clinically non-specific features. We show that
a matched-control design with external transfer can separate
pathway claims that remain anatomically specific and exter￾nally consistent from those that do not, and can identify cases
where target perturbation alone would produce misleading
conclusions. The protocol also reveals that the perturbation
operator itself is a critical methodological variable: zero￾masking, the most common occlusion method in the lit￾erature, creates hard-boundary artifacts that inflate control￾region disruption and can reverse specificity conclusions. A
continuity-preserving operator (linear interpolation) eliminates
this artifact and provides more conservative, anatomically
interpretable ASS estimates. The protocol thus addresses a
gap between standard discrimination benchmarks (which mea￾sure only predictive accuracy) and pathway-specific evidence
(which requires evidence about how models arrive at deci￾sions).
II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
and reconstruction-based perturbation strategies [26], [27],
and Shapley-value-based ablation [28] to quantify localized
feature importance in ECG classifiers. Beyond ECG, Ross
et al. [29] demonstrated that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion, providing an alternative to post-hoc auditing—though

Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden
data acquisition biases in ECG datasets can inflate model
performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90
to 0.70 under external validation. In medical imaging more
broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].
These features define distinct diagnostic pathways for condi￾tions such as 1AVB (prolonged PR>200ms), bundle branch
blocks (wide QRS>120ms with characteristic terminal/lateral
R patterns), sinus bradycardia (low ventricular rate), and atrial
fibrillation (absent or fibrillatory atrial activity).
Recent studies have directly tested whether deep ECG
models learn these clinically meaningful features. Hempel et
al. [39] extended an XAI framework to match deep learning
relevances with PR interval and QRS duration from PTB-XL+,
reporting that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms and 98.6% of high-confidence LBBB predictions
had QRS>120ms—strong evidence that the model internally
represents clinical thresholds. Riberg et al. [40] performed a
concordance analysis between ResNet predictions and cardi￾ology guideline thresholds, finding that RR interval features
dominated for sinus bradycardia and tachycardia while mor￾phological features showed weaker correlation. Hammer et
al. [41] introduced an architecture that explicitly separates
rhythm (long-term) and morphology (short-term) processing,
demonstrating that fused explanations correlate with clinical
diagnostic criteria. A systematic review by Ayano et al. [42]
confirmed that interpretable ML studies for ECG increasingly
target clinical parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration,
and RR variability.
Despite this progress, a critical gap remains: existing studies
confirm that models attend to clinically relevant features,
but they do not test whether a disease-specific signal region
dominates over anatomically adjacent controls, or whether
such pathway specificity survives dataset shift. Demonstrating
feature relevance is not the same as demonstrating feature
specificity. Our disease-centered, matched-control perturbation
audit addresses this gap: for five diagnoses spanning timing,
morphology, and rhythm pathways, we pre-specify expected
positive regions grounded in clinical physiology, compare
targeted perturbations against matched controls, and verify
pathway specificity under frozen-weight external transfer. This

III. METHODS
A. Study Overview: Matched-Control Pathway Audit
Standard discrimination metrics (AUROC, F1) cannot dis￾tinguish a model that uses disease-relevant signal regions from
one that exploits statistically correlated but mechanistically
irrelevant shortcuts. Our matched-control pathway audit proto￾col is designed to make this distinction explicit. The protocol
proceeds in four stages, summarized in Fig. 1:
1) Disease-centered audit panel: For each of five diag￾noses spanning timing (1AVB), morphology (CRBBB,
CLBBB), and rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB) pathways, we
pre-specify an expected positive pathway grounded in
clinical ECG diagnostic criteria, anatomically matched
control regions, and any ambiguous pathway treated as
hypothesis-testing (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator—linear interpolation, selected via a preregis￾tered four-operator comparison battery—is applied to
both the target region and each matched control. Per￾turbations fall into two classes: local window perturba￾tion for temporally localized features (e.g., PR interval,
QRS complex), and global signal transformation for
distributed properties (e.g., heart rate, RR variability).
The matched-control design is the protocol’s core safe￾guard: a pathway claim requires the target perturbation
to be more disruptive than its strongest matched control,
not merely that the target perturbation produces a large
effect (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: The Anatomical
Specificity Score (ASS) operationalizes the matched￾control comparison as a single scalar. Cross-Dataset
Direction Consistency (CDDC) checks whether the sign
of ASS is preserved under external transfer. Each (ar￾chitecture, disease) pair is assigned to one of three
evidence tiers—Pathway-supported, Evidence-limited,
or Not supported—under a predefined primary opera￾tor. Tier boundaries are conservative by design (Sec￾tion III-E).
4) External validation: Frozen-weight transfer from
CODE-15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10
provides an external check on whether pathway conclu￾sions are dataset-specific (Section III-B).
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation win￾dows, matched-control comparisons, and evaluation metrics
apply to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input. We
demonstrate this by instantiating the audit across four archi￾tectures at three representation levels (Section III-F), with
external validation on an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset. The five diagnoses serve as a case-study panel chosen
to span three clinically distinct diagnostic pathway categories,
not as an exhaustive clinical survey.
B. Datasets and External Validation Setting
CODE-15% (internal audit cohort): Brazilian ECG
dataset with 345,779 12-lead exams (400Hz, 10-second du￾ration) from 233,770 patients [6]. Labels were derived from
an automated ECG interpretation system. We use five tar￾get conditions spanning three diagnostic pathways: 1AVB
(timing), CRBBB/CLBBB (morphology), and SBRAD/AFIB
(rhythm). Their prevalences are 1.65%, 2.80%, 1.74%, 1.62%,
and 2.03%, respectively. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232
samples), 20% validation (69,045 samples), 20% test (69,520
samples), random seed 42.
Label circularity risk: Because CODE-15% labels are
automated rather than physician-adjudicated, models trained
on them may learn to replicate the automated labeling logic
instead of recovering physician-level diagnostic mechanisms.
The risk varies by disease: 1AVB (highest, PR>200ms
threshold overlap), SBRAD (high, heart-rate-based rules),
CRBBB/CLBBB (moderate, QRS morphology criteria may
align with automated feature extraction), and AFIB (moderate,
atrial activity metrics may overlap with rhythm classifier
components). We treat PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist-validated
labels) as the primary external credibility buffer, and we
recommend interpreting internal CODE findings as evidence
about model behavior relative to the automated-label system,
not as evidence of physician-level diagnostic reasoning.
PTB-XL (external validation cohort): German ECG
dataset with 21,837 records from 18,885 patients at 500Hz [5].
We use the official patient-level folds: folds 1–8 for reference,
fold 9 (n = 2, 183) for target-domain threshold retuning, and
fold 10 (n = 2, 198) for testing. Fold 10 labels were validated
by cardiologists and serve as the primary external credibility
set. SCP-ECG diagnostic codes were mapped to the five target
diseases using strict primary code matching. For frozen-model
external validation, PTB-XL signals were downsampled from
500Hz to 400Hz via Fourier resampling to match CODE-15%
input rate, then trimmed/padded to 4,096 samples (10.24s).
Z-score normalization was applied per lead with lead or￾der (I, II, III, AVR, AVL, AVF, V1–V6) matching CODE￾15% ordering. External evaluation uses three transfer levels
to bound the frozen-model performance: (1) strict frozen—
CODE validation thresholds applied directly to PTB-XL fold
10; (2) calibrated transfer—thresholds retuned on PTB-XL
fold 9; (3) oracle upper bound—optimal thresholds computed
directly on fold 10. AUROC is threshold-invariant and serves
as the primary frozen-generalization metric.

D. Perturbation Design
The perturbation audit applies two classes of signal interven￾tion depending on whether the diagnostic feature is localized
in time or distributed across the recording. All perturbations
share a common operator (linear interpolation, Section III-D1),
matched-subset construction (equal-sized positive/negative co￾horts, random seed 42), and uncertainty quantification (patient￾level bootstrap, n = 1, 000 iterations). Perturbation is applied
across all 12 leads for local-window targets; for random￾window controls, 5 random placements per exam are averaged
via logit averaging.
1) Perturbation Operator Selection: For each perturbation
target and matched control, a predefined temporal window
is centered relative to each detected R-peak. We use linear
interpolation as the primary perturbation operator: the signal
segment within the window is replaced by a straight-line
interpolation between the two boundary values (Fig. 2B–C),
preserving local waveform continuity and avoiding the hard
discontinuities introduced by zero-masking (Fig. 2D–F). The
operator is simple, deterministic, and applies identically to
target and control windows.

E. Audit Metrics and Evidence Tiers
The audit interpretation centers on two primary metrics
derived from matched perturbation results, plus a set of
secondary summaries.
Anatomical Specificity Score (ASS) — the primary audit
metric — compares the target pathway against its strongest
matched control:
ASS(d, f) = ∆AUROCtarget(d, f) − max
c∈Cf
∆AUROCc(d).
A positive ASS indicates the target perturbation is more
disruptive than any matched control; a negative ASS indicates
at least one control is more disruptive. ∆AUROC denotes the
change in AUROC from clean to perturbed signals (positive
values indicate degradation). ASS is computed under the pri￾mary linear-interpolation operator for all pathway-specificity
claims.
Cross-Dataset Direction Consistency (CDDC) checks
whether ASS has the same sign on CODE-15% and PTB￾XL fold 10, reported with bootstrap-based direction stability.
AUROC is threshold-invariant and serves as the primary metric
for cross-dataset comparisons.
Secondary metrics: Pathway Sensitivity Score (PSS)
measures raw clean-to-target degradation (AUROCclean −
AUROCtarget). Knowledge Alignment Score (KAS), reported
in Supplementary Material, summarizes whether expected
positive pathways dominate control pathways at the disease
level.
1) Evidence-Classification Rules: A preregistered com￾parison of perturbation operators (Supplementary Material)
demonstrates that pathway conclusions depend critically on
the perturbation operator. To prevent operator selection from
becoming a post-hoc degree of freedom, we pre-specify an
evidence-classification framework that constrains what can
be claimed under each pattern of evidence. Linear interpola￾tion is predefined as the primary operator; zero-masking and
beat-conditioned inpainting results are retained for operator￾sensitivity disclosure only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa￾tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤ 0 under the
primary operator.
These tiers constrain the vocabulary used throughout the
paper. Tier boundaries are conservative by design: positive ev￾idence under a deprecated operator does not override primary￾operator results. Cross-architecture consistency is reported as
a qualitative finding, preserving the model-level audit focus.

G. Statistical Analysis
Uncertainty quantification: Patient-level bootstrap confi￾dence intervals (1,000 replicates, seed 42) are the primary
uncertainty quantification throughout this paper [44]. For
the perturbation audit, bootstrap replicates resample patients
(not individual ECGs) with replacement; all ECGs belonging
to a resampled patient are included, preserving the within￾patient correlation structure. ASS is computed on the paired
target-versus-control perturbation effects within each replicate,
maintaining the matched-subject design.
Model comparison: Pairwise model comparisons (ResNet
vs XGBoost Simple, ResNet vs XGBoost Clinical-MVP, XG￾Boost Clinical-MVP vs Simple) were performed per disease
on the shared test set. For AUROC, we used the DeLong
test [45] for paired comparisons on identical test samples.
For F1, we used vectorized paired permutation tests with
5,000 resamples [46]. Two-sided p-values were computed as
the proportion of |permuted ∆F1| ≥ |observed ∆F1|. Holm￾Bonferroni correction was applied to the family of 18 compar￾isons (3 model pairs × 5 diseases + 3 macro-F1). We note that
permutation p-values and DeLong tests operate at the sample
level (n ≈ 69, 500 ECGs from approximately 47,000 unique
patients; mean 1.48 samples/patient); because within-patient
correlations reduce the effective sample size, sample-level tests
may produce optimistic p-values and are reported for com￾pleteness as approximate secondary indicators. Patient-level
bootstrap CIs provide the primary uncertainty quantification.
Multiplicity control for external pathway tests: The
primary external audit tests 15 pre-specified hypotheses of
the form H0 : ASS ≤ 0 (one-sided) under the primary

Before applying the perturbation audit, we establish base￾line classification performance to demonstrate that all models

I. INTRODUCTION
Deep learning classifiers for electrocardiogram (ECG) anal￾ysis now achieve high discrimination across a growing set of
cardiac conditions [1]–[4], aided by large public datasets such
as PTB-XL [5] and CODE-15% [6]. But strong discrimination
does not tell us whether a model relies on disease-relevant
signal regions—a gap that matters for clinical deployment
beyond benchmark performance. A 1AVB classifier might
depend on QRS morphology instead of PR-interval timing; an
AFIB classifier might use ventricular rate irregularity, atrial
waveform features, or unrelated shortcuts. Standard bench￾mark metrics cannot distinguish these cases. Moreover, exist￾ing explanation methods rarely test whether disease-relevant
regions dominate over matched controls, or whether pathway
dependence holds up under dataset shift—sensitivity is not
specificity, and explanation conclusions can be fragile under
distribution shift [7], [8].
We address these gaps with a model-agnostic, matched￾control perturbation audit protocol. For each diagnosis we pre￾specify an expected positive pathway (e.g., the PR segment
for 1AVB, the QRS complex for bundle branch block) and
compare targeted perturbations against anatomically adjacent
control regions that should matter less. A pathway claim is
accepted only if the target perturbation is more disruptive
than its strongest matched control—a stricter criterion than
perturbation sensitivity alone. We further evaluate pathway
specificity under frozen-weight transfer from CODE-15% to
cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, providing an external
check on whether explanation conclusions are dataset-specific.
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation design
applies to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input, and

II. RELATED WORK
A. ECG Classification with Deep Learning
1D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and residual
architectures have become the dominant paradigm for auto￾mated ECG classification. Hannun et al. [1] demonstrated
cardiologist-level arrhythmia detection using a 34-layer 1D
CNN on ambulatory ECGs. On the PTB-XL benchmark,
Strodthoff et al. [2] established strong baselines with 1D
ResNets and fully convolutional networks across 71 diagnostic
classes; their follow-up review [3] confirmed that ResNet-style
architectures remain competitive against newer alternatives.
Mehari and Strodthoff [9] further advanced PTB-XL bench￾marks through self-supervised pre-training, while Chen et
al. [10] and Zubair et al. [11] contributed targeted architectures
for multi-class and imbalanced ECG classification.
Beyond vanilla ResNets, SE-ResNet [12] adds channel-wise
attention, and lightweight Transformer adaptations [13] have
been applied via patch-based self-attention. Recent hybrid
architectures combine these paradigms—Cardioformer [14]
couples multi-granularity patching with Transformer layers,
while xECGArch [15] separates morphology and rhythm pro￾cessing with dual CNNs. ECG-JEPA [16] pushed PTB-XL
performance to AUROC=0.945 through JEPA pre-training
on over one million records spanning ten datasets including
CODE-15%. Foundation models such as ECG-FM [17] fur￾ther scale pre-training, though their explanation behavior and
pathway-level auditability remain unexplored. Prior to the deep
learning era, classical machine learning methods—including
XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines—
were widely applied to handcrafted ECG features and remain
competitive baselines on structured feature sets [18], [19].
Despite these advances across both classical and deep
learning paradigms, the common evaluation framework em￾phasizes discrimination metrics on held-out test splits. It
remains unclear whether these models base their decisions
on disease-relevant signal regions, and whether region-specific
dependence survives cross-dataset transfer. This gap motivates
our multi-level audit protocol, which applies identical pathway
questions across representation levels—from a feature-based
XGBoost baseline to a raw-signal ResNet—allowing us to
assess pathway dependence across both classical and deep
learning models.
B. Explainability and Perturbation Methods
Post-hoc explanation methods—including saliency maps,
occlusion-based sensitivity, guided backpropagation, and in￾tegrated gradients—have been systematically evaluated on
ECG tasks. Storas et al. [20] compared nine gradient-based ˚
methods on synthetic 12-lead ECGs and found that no single
method works best across all measurement tasks, with con￾siderable disagreement between human expert evaluation and
perturbation-based metrics. Suh et al. [21] evaluated eleven
attribution methods across five large ECG datasets and re￾ported that Guided Grad-CAM best aligned with cardiologists’
assessment while localization-based metrics better reflected
human judgment than perturbation-based ones. Plagwitz et
al. [22] assessed the reliability of feature attribution explana￾tions in ECG analysis through systematic perturbation testing,
reporting that explanation reliability varies substantially across
attribution methods and disease categories. Al-Zaiti et al. [23]
found that clinically deployed saliency maps for occlusion
MI detection were rated only slightly clinically relevant by
practicing clinicians, underscoring the gap between current
explanation quality and clinical expectations.
Perturbation-based evaluation—in which input regions are
removed or altered to measure prediction change—provides
a more direct test of feature dependence than gradient-based
attributions alone. Wagner et al. [24] proposed a structured
XAI framework for ECG that combines occlusion-based san￾ity checks, glocal attribution aggregation, and concept-based
analysis, providing quantitative evidence that model behav￾ior can align with cardiologists’ decision rules. Bender et
al. [25] demonstrated that a ResNet trained for 12-lead ECG
classification learns features analogous to clinical diagnostic
criteria including P-wave morphology, QRS duration, and
PR interval. Recent work has also applied wave masking
and reconstruction-based perturbation strategies [26], [27],
and Shapley-value-based ablation [28] to quantify localized
feature importance in ECG classifiers. Beyond ECG, Ross
et al. [29] demonstrated that constraining models to produce
“right” explanations during training can improve generaliza￾tion, providing an alternative to post-hoc auditing—though

Despite these advances, three structural limitations persist
across the existing ECG explanation literature. First, existing
perturbation studies rarely incorporate matched anatomical
controls: they test whether a region matters, but not whether
disease-specific regions matter more than adjacent control
regions. This is the key distinction between perturbation
sensitivity (a region is important) and anatomical specificity (a
disease-specific region is more important than its anatomically
adjacent controls)—a distinction we operationalize through the
ASS metric and matched-control design. Second, explanation
conclusions are typically validated only within the training
distribution. Adebayo et al. [7] showed that saliency maps
can fail basic sanity checks under simple input transfor￾mations, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola [30] demonstrated that
interpretability methods can be fragile under input pertur￾bations, and Ong Ly et al. [31] demonstrated that hidden
data acquisition biases in ECG datasets can inflate model
performance by up to 20%, with AUROC dropping from 0.90
to 0.70 under external validation. In medical imaging more
broadly, DeGrave et al. [32] showed that deep learning models
for radiographic COVID-19 detection selected clinically irrele￾vant shortcuts over meaningful signal—a finding that directly
parallels our concern about ECG classifiers exploiting non￾specific waveform features. Third, few studies test whether
explanation claims survive external dataset shift [8]. These
gaps directly motivate our matched-control perturbation design
with frozen-weight cross-dataset transfer.
C. Dataset Use and Cross-Dataset Validation
The two largest public 12-lead ECG datasets—PTB-XL [5]
(21,837 records, cardiologist-validated labels) and CODE-15%
[6] (345,779 exams, automated labels)—have enabled a wide
range of deep learning studies. PTB-XL provides carefully
annotated multi-label diagnoses with rich metadata including
signal quality indicators and demographic attributes, while
CODE-15% offers an order of magnitude more samples but
with labels derived from an automated interpretation system.
This label-source asymmetry introduces a critical distinction:
models trained on CODE-15% may learn to replicate the
automated labeling logic rather than physician-level diagnostic
features, creating a label circularity risk that varies by disease
category. The PTB-XL+ dataset [33] supplements PTB-XL
with 71 handcrafted features spanning heart rate variability,
QRS morphology, and signal quality metrics, enabling direct
comparisons between learned representations and classical
ECG parameters.
Cross-dataset validation remains underutilized in the ECG
deep learning literature, and where it has been attempted,
the results are sobering. Bickmann et al. [18] benchmarked
time-series versus feature-based methods on PTB-XL but
did not include external validation. Soltanieh et al. [34]
addressed out-of-distribution generalization for self-supervised
ECG representations, showing that dataset shift degrades stan￾dard supervised baselines. Frank et al. [35] reported that
models achieving AUROC>0.90 within-dataset for myocardial
ischemia detection experienced substantial performance drops
across six public ECG databases. At the foundation-model
scale, ECGFounder [36] and recent benchmarking efforts [37]
confirm that cross-domain generalization remains a key chal￾lenge even for large pre-trained models with diverse training
data.
The consistent picture is that external validation across
datasets with different label sources, populations, and acqui￾sition protocols is widely recommended but rarely executed,
and even less often applied to explanation claims. Our study
addresses this gap through frozen-weight transfer from CODE￾15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10, treating the
external dataset as a simultaneous check on both prediction
quality and pathway explanation consistency.
D. Clinical Pathway and Mechanistic Analysis
Clinical ECG interpretation relies on well-defined phys￾iological features: PR interval for atrioventricular conduc￾tion timing, QRS duration and morphology for ventricular
conduction, RR interval regularity for rhythm classification,
and P-wave morphology for atrial activity assessment [38].
These features define distinct diagnostic pathways for condi￾tions such as 1AVB (prolonged PR>200ms), bundle branch
blocks (wide QRS>120ms with characteristic terminal/lateral
R patterns), sinus bradycardia (low ventricular rate), and atrial
fibrillation (absent or fibrillatory atrial activity).
Recent studies have directly tested whether deep ECG
models learn these clinically meaningful features. Hempel et
al. [39] extended an XAI framework to match deep learning
relevances with PR interval and QRS duration from PTB-XL+,
reporting that 96.0% of high-confidence 1AVB predictions had
PR>200ms and 98.6% of high-confidence LBBB predictions
had QRS>120ms—strong evidence that the model internally
represents clinical thresholds. Riberg et al. [40] performed a
concordance analysis between ResNet predictions and cardi￾ology guideline thresholds, finding that RR interval features
dominated for sinus bradycardia and tachycardia while mor￾phological features showed weaker correlation. Hammer et
al. [41] introduced an architecture that explicitly separates
rhythm (long-term) and morphology (short-term) processing,
demonstrating that fused explanations correlate with clinical
diagnostic criteria. A systematic review by Ayano et al. [42]
confirmed that interpretable ML studies for ECG increasingly
target clinical parameters such as PR interval, QRS duration,
and RR variability.
Despite this progress, a critical gap remains: existing studies
confirm that models attend to clinically relevant features,
but they do not test whether a disease-specific signal region
dominates over anatomically adjacent controls, or whether
such pathway specificity survives dataset shift. Demonstrating
feature relevance is not the same as demonstrating feature
specificity. Our disease-centered, matched-control perturbation
audit addresses this gap: for five diagnoses spanning timing,
morphology, and rhythm pathways, we pre-specify expected
positive regions grounded in clinical physiology, compare
targeted perturbations against matched controls, and verify
pathway specificity under frozen-weight external transfer. This

III. METHODS
A. Study Overview: Matched-Control Pathway Audit
Standard discrimination metrics (AUROC, F1) cannot dis￾tinguish a model that uses disease-relevant signal regions from
one that exploits statistically correlated but mechanistically
irrelevant shortcuts. Our matched-control pathway audit proto￾col is designed to make this distinction explicit. The protocol
proceeds in four stages, summarized in Fig. 1:
1) Disease-centered audit panel: For each of five diag￾noses spanning timing (1AVB), morphology (CRBBB,
CLBBB), and rhythm (SBRAD, AFIB) pathways, we
pre-specify an expected positive pathway grounded in
clinical ECG diagnostic criteria, anatomically matched
control regions, and any ambiguous pathway treated as
hypothesis-testing (Section III-C).
2) Matched-control perturbation: The same perturbation
operator—linear interpolation, selected via a preregis￾tered four-operator comparison battery—is applied to
both the target region and each matched control. Per￾turbations fall into two classes: local window perturba￾tion for temporally localized features (e.g., PR interval,
QRS complex), and global signal transformation for
distributed properties (e.g., heart rate, RR variability).
The matched-control design is the protocol’s core safe￾guard: a pathway claim requires the target perturbation
to be more disruptive than its strongest matched control,
not merely that the target perturbation produces a large
effect (Section III-D).
3) Audit metrics and evidence tiers: The Anatomical
Specificity Score (ASS) operationalizes the matched￾control comparison as a single scalar. Cross-Dataset
Direction Consistency (CDDC) checks whether the sign
of ASS is preserved under external transfer. Each (ar￾chitecture, disease) pair is assigned to one of three
evidence tiers—Pathway-supported, Evidence-limited,
or Not supported—under a predefined primary opera￾tor. Tier boundaries are conservative by design (Sec￾tion III-E).
4) External validation: Frozen-weight transfer from
CODE-15% to cardiologist-validated PTB-XL fold 10
provides an external check on whether pathway conclu￾sions are dataset-specific (Section III-B).
The protocol is model-agnostic: the same perturbation win￾dows, matched-control comparisons, and evaluation metrics
apply to any classifier accepting 12-lead ECG input. We
demonstrate this by instantiating the audit across four archi￾tectures at three representation levels (Section III-F), with
external validation on an independent cardiologist-validated
dataset. The five diagnoses serve as a case-study panel chosen
to span three clinically distinct diagnostic pathway categories,
not as an exhaustive clinical survey.
B. Datasets and External Validation Setting
CODE-15% (internal audit cohort): Brazilian ECG
dataset with 345,779 12-lead exams (400Hz, 10-second du￾ration) from 233,770 patients [6]. Labels were derived from
an automated ECG interpretation system. We use five tar￾get conditions spanning three diagnostic pathways: 1AVB
(timing), CRBBB/CLBBB (morphology), and SBRAD/AFIB
(rhythm). Their prevalences are 1.65%, 2.80%, 1.74%, 1.62%,
and 2.03%, respectively. Patient-level split: 60% train (207,232
samples), 20% validation (69,045 samples), 20% test (69,520
samples), random seed 42.
Label circularity risk: Because CODE-15% labels are
automated rather than physician-adjudicated, models trained
on them may learn to replicate the automated labeling logic
instead of recovering physician-level diagnostic mechanisms.
The risk varies by disease: 1AVB (highest, PR>200ms
threshold overlap), SBRAD (high, heart-rate-based rules),
CRBBB/CLBBB (moderate, QRS morphology criteria may
align with automated feature extraction), and AFIB (moderate,
atrial activity metrics may overlap with rhythm classifier
components). We treat PTB-XL fold 10 (cardiologist-validated
labels) as the primary external credibility buffer, and we
recommend interpreting internal CODE findings as evidence
about model behavior relative to the automated-label system,
not as evidence of physician-level diagnostic reasoning.
PTB-XL (external validation cohort): German ECG
dataset with 21,837 records from 18,885 patients at 500Hz [5].
We use the official patient-level folds: folds 1–8 for reference,
fold 9 (n = 2, 183) for target-domain threshold retuning, and
fold 10 (n = 2, 198) for testing. Fold 10 labels were validated
by cardiologists and serve as the primary external credibility
set. SCP-ECG diagnostic codes were mapped to the five target
diseases using strict primary code matching. For frozen-model
external validation, PTB-XL signals were downsampled from
500Hz to 400Hz via Fourier resampling to match CODE-15%
input rate, then trimmed/padded to 4,096 samples (10.24s).
Z-score normalization was applied per lead with lead or￾der (I, II, III, AVR, AVL, AVF, V1–V6) matching CODE￾15% ordering. External evaluation uses three transfer levels
to bound the frozen-model performance: (1) strict frozen—
CODE validation thresholds applied directly to PTB-XL fold
10; (2) calibrated transfer—thresholds retuned on PTB-XL
fold 9; (3) oracle upper bound—optimal thresholds computed
directly on fold 10. AUROC is threshold-invariant and serves
as the primary frozen-generalization metric.

E. Audit Metrics and Evidence Tiers
The audit interpretation centers on two primary metrics
derived from matched perturbation results, plus a set of
secondary summaries.
Anatomical Specificity Score (ASS) — the primary audit
metric — compares the target pathway against its strongest
matched control:
ASS(d, f) = ∆AUROCtarget(d, f) − max
c∈Cf
∆AUROCc(d).
A positive ASS indicates the target perturbation is more
disruptive than any matched control; a negative ASS indicates
at least one control is more disruptive. ∆AUROC denotes the
change in AUROC from clean to perturbed signals (positive
values indicate degradation). ASS is computed under the pri￾mary linear-interpolation operator for all pathway-specificity
claims.
Cross-Dataset Direction Consistency (CDDC) checks
whether ASS has the same sign on CODE-15% and PTB￾XL fold 10, reported with bootstrap-based direction stability.
AUROC is threshold-invariant and serves as the primary metric
for cross-dataset comparisons.
Secondary metrics: Pathway Sensitivity Score (PSS)
measures raw clean-to-target degradation (AUROCclean −
AUROCtarget). Knowledge Alignment Score (KAS), reported
in Supplementary Material, summarizes whether expected
positive pathways dominate control pathways at the disease
level.
1) Evidence-Classification Rules: A preregistered com￾parison of perturbation operators (Supplementary Material)
demonstrates that pathway conclusions depend critically on
the perturbation operator. To prevent operator selection from
becoming a post-hoc degree of freedom, we pre-specify an
evidence-classification framework that constrains what can
be claimed under each pattern of evidence. Linear interpola￾tion is predefined as the primary operator; zero-masking and
beat-conditioned inpainting results are retained for operator￾sensitivity disclosure only.
Evidence tiers. The audit targets individual models: the
same disease-pathway pair may yield different conclusions for
different architectures, and this heterogeneity is itself informa￾tive. Tiers are assigned per (architecture, disease-pathway) pair
under the primary operator:
1) Pathway-supported: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI
lower bound > 0 on this model internally. External
ASS (when available for this model under the primary
operator) maintains the same direction with CI lower
bound > 0.
2) Evidence-limited: Primary-operator ASS> 0 with CI>
0 on this model internally, but external primary-operator
evidence is not yet available for this model, OR external
CI crosses zero.
3) Not supported: This model yields ASS≤ 0 under the
primary operator.
These tiers constrain the vocabulary used throughout the
paper. Tier boundaries are conservative by design: positive ev￾idence under a deprecated operator does not override primary￾operator results. Cross-architecture consistency is reported as
a qualitative finding, preserving the model-level audit focus.

G. Statistical Analysis
Uncertainty quantification: Patient-level bootstrap confi￾dence intervals (1,000 replicates, seed 42) are the primary
uncertainty quantification throughout this paper [44]. For
the perturbation audit, bootstrap replicates resample patients
(not individual ECGs) with replacement; all ECGs belonging
to a resampled patient are included, preserving the within￾patient correlation structure. ASS is computed on the paired
target-versus-control perturbation effects within each replicate,
maintaining the matched-subject design.
Model comparison: Pairwise model comparisons (ResNet
vs XGBoost Simple, ResNet vs XGBoost Clinical-MVP, XG￾Boost Clinical-MVP vs Simple) were performed per disease
on the shared test set. For AUROC, we used the DeLong
test [45] for paired comparisons on identical test samples.
For F1, we used vectorized paired permutation tests with
5,000 resamples [46]. Two-sided p-values were computed as
the proportion of |permuted ∆F1| ≥ |observed ∆F1|. Holm￾Bonferroni correction was applied to the family of 18 compar￾isons (3 model pairs × 5 diseases + 3 macro-F1). We note that
permutation p-values and DeLong tests operate at the sample
level (n ≈ 69, 500 ECGs from approximately 47,000 unique
patients; mean 1.48 samples/patient); because within-patient
correlations reduce the effective sample size, sample-level tests
may produce optimistic p-values and are reported for com￾pleteness as approximate secondary indicators. Patient-level
bootstrap CIs provide the primary uncertainty quantification.
Multiplicity control for external pathway tests: The
primary external audit tests 15 pre-specified hypotheses of
the form H0 : ASS ≤ 0 (one-sided) under the primary
linear-interpolation operator on PTB-XL fold 10. We apply
the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) pro￾cedure at α = 0.05 to control the expected proportion of false

Before applying the perturbation audit, we establish base￾line classification performance to demonstrate that all models
achieve high discrimination—and that this fact alone reveals
nothing about whether a model uses disease-relevant signal
regions rather than correlated shortcuts. This section is inten￾tionally brief; the core contribution begins with the matched￾control perturbation audit in Section IV-B.
All five diseases achieve AUROC> 0.98 on ResNet (Ta￾ble IV), with Micro-F1= 0.736. SE-ResNet is statistically

## 建议 Methods 改成这个大纲

### III. METHODS

### A. Study Design and Audit Logic  
这一节只回答：**我们的方法整体在干什么。**

建议写成三句话主线：

1. 常规 discrimination metrics 不能判断模型是否用了医学上相关的 signal pathway。  
2. 所以我们提出 matched-control pathway audit：目标 pathway 的扰动效果必须超过最强 matched control。  
3. 最后用外部数据集 frozen-weight transfer 检查 pathway conclusion 是否能跨数据集成立。

这里保留你现在的四阶段概述，但可以压缩。现在这部分其实写得不错，问题是后面没有始终围绕它组织。

---

### B. Datasets and Transfer Setting  
这一节放数据集，不要混入太多解释性讨论。

内容顺序建议：

1. CODE-15%：训练 / 内部 audit 数据集  
2. PTB-XL fold 10：外部验证数据集  
3. preprocessing：采样率、长度、lead order、normalization  
4. frozen transfer setting：strict frozen / calibrated / oracle  
5. label circularity risk：放在最后，作为解释限制

你现在 Dataset 部分信息是有价值的，尤其 CODE-15% 自动标签和 PTB-XL 心内科医生验证标签的差异，这能支撑 external validation 的必要性 fileciteturn1file0。但建议不要在这里写得太像 Discussion，点到即可。

### C. Disease-Centered Pathway Definitions  
这一节回答：**五个疾病各自的医学 target pathway 和 matched controls 是什么。**

这里建议直接保留 Table I，并在正文里只讲设计原则：

1. target region 来自临床 ECG 诊断标准  
2. matched controls 是解剖相邻但机制不同的区域  
3. ambiguous pathway 不强行假设，而是作为 hypothesis-testing

你现在 Table I 很重要，1AVB、CRBBB、CLBBB、SBRAD、AFIB 的 expected pathway / controls / ambiguous pathway 都已经列清楚了 fileciteturn1file3。但正文可以更短，不要重复表格。

### D. Perturbation Protocol  
这一节是 Methods 的核心，但现在略显杂。建议拆成三个小节：

#### D1. Primary Perturbation Operator  
先讲为什么用 linear interpolation。

这里可以写：

- 所有 target 和 controls 使用同一个 operator；
- primary operator 是 linear interpolation；
- 选择原因是 continuity-preserving，避免 zero-masking 的 hard-boundary artifact；
- zero-masking 和 beat-conditioned inpainting 只作为 sensitivity disclosure，不进入 primary tiering。

这个逻辑你现在已经写了，尤其提到 linear interpolation 保持局部连续性、zero-masking 会引入 hard discontinuities fileciteturn1file3。但我建议不要在 Methods 主文里反复强调“preregistered four-operator battery”的细节，把细节放 Supplement，否则主线会被 operator comparison 抢走。

#### D2. Local Window Perturbation  
放 1AVB、CRBBB、CLBBB、AFIB atrial-window。

#### D3. Global Transformation  
放 SBRAD 和 AFIB RR regularization。

这里要特别注意：**SBRAD 是 global target + local controls 的 hybrid design**，AFIB 同时有 atrial-window 和 RR regularization。这个地方如果不讲清楚，读者会觉得 AFIB/SBRAD 的 protocol 和前面的 local perturbation 不是同一种东西。

这一节回答：**扰动之后怎么判定 supported / not supported。**

2. ASS：target drop − strongest control drop  
3. CDDC：internal 和 external 是否同方向

## 我建议你重点改的地方

第一，**把 operator comparison 降权**。它很重要，但它是“为什么选 linear interpolation”的支撑，不应该在 Methods 主文里抢走 audit protocol 的主线。现在读者可能会觉得你一会儿在讲 matched-control，一会儿在讲 operator artifact，焦点有点飘。

第二，**把模型部分压缩**。Methods 里模型细节过多，会让文章看起来像“我训练了很多模型”，而不是“我提出了一个 audit framework”。SE-ResNet 和 Transformer 应该明确写成 architecture sensitivity checks，而不是并列贡献。

第三，**把 AFIB 和 SBRAD 的 protocol 讲得更层次化**。因为它们不是单纯 local-window perturbation，容易让审稿人觉得方法不统一。你要主动说：local pathway 和 global pathway 对应不同 intervention class，这是设计选择，不是临时拼接。

第四，**检查 Fig. 1**。你现在 Fig. 1 页面里还有红色批注，而且图中 “Supportive evidence / Narrow support / Transfer-stressed” 这类措辞和正文的三档 evidence tier 不完全一致。这个很危险，Methods 里既然已经定义了 Pathway-supported / Evidence-limited / Not supported，图也必须完全统一。否则审稿人会觉得分类标准前后不一致。

总的来说：**Methods 不是散到不能用，但现在像“把所有方法材料都放进来了”，还不是“围绕一个审稿人能复述的 protocol 组织起来”。** 你要把它改成：先定义 audit 问题，再定义 disease pathway，再定义 perturbation，再定义判定规则，最后才是模型和统计。这样读起来会清楚很多。
